seo_title: Xactimate vs Contractor Estimates: Why the Numbers Differ
meta_description: Xactimate vs contractor estimates: how each is built, why they rarely match, and how Texas owners reconcile the gap.
h1: Xactimate vs Contractor Estimates: Why They Differ and How to Resolve It
secondary_keywords: why is my Xactimate estimate low
excerpt: Why do Xactimate and contractor estimates rarely match? Learn how each is built, the scope and pricing gaps behind the difference, and how to reconcile them on a Texas claim.
key_takeaways: Xactimate values the loss with regional price lists; contractors price real costs.
Scope gaps, waste, pricing dates and overhead and profit drive most differences.
Itemized contractor estimates are much harder for adjusters to dismiss.
Compare estimates line by line and support each difference with evidence.
Appraisal resolves amount-of-loss disputes when coverage is accepted.
body_html:
Xactimate vs contractor estimates comes down to purpose and pricing. Xactimate is estimating software insurers use to price repairs line by line from regional price lists. A contractor estimate reflects what that contractor will actually charge, based on real crew, supplier and site costs. They often differ because of scope gaps, pricing assumptions, waste, overhead and profit and code items.

What is Xactimate?

Xactimate is property estimating software developed by Xactware, a Verisk business. It is the most widely used estimating platform in the U.S. property insurance industry. Adjusters use it to build estimates by selecting line items, such as "remove and replace laminated comp shingles" or "paint drywall, two coats," and entering quantities. The software applies unit prices from a price list for the property's area.

How Xactimate pricing works

Xactimate price lists are built from market research on labor, materials and equipment and are updated regularly, often monthly, by region. Each unit price bundles materials, labor and sometimes equipment for that task.

Pricing factorHow it affects Xactimate estimates
Labor ratesVary by trade and region
Material costsChange as supplier pricing moves
EquipmentRental rates for lifts, dumpsters and safety gear
Market conditionsPost-storm demand may lag behind real prices
Price list dateAn older list may not reflect current costs

For a deeper look, read how Xactimate pricing works in Texas and why Xactimate estimates differ by ZIP code.

Who uses Xactimate?

  • Staff and independent insurance adjusters
  • Public adjusters
  • Roofing and restoration contractors who work insurance claims
  • Insurance appraisers and umpires

Because so many parties use it, Xactimate acts as a common language for claims. That makes it easier to compare estimates item by item, which is a big advantage in a dispute. It also means the quality of an Xactimate estimate depends heavily on who writes it and how thoroughly they inspected the property.

Xactimate vs Symbility

Symbility is another claims estimating platform used by some insurers. It works on a similar principle: line items, quantities and regional pricing. The comparison issues are the same, so everything in this guide about Xactimate vs contractor estimates applies to Symbility estimates too. Appraisers and estimators who work in both platforms can translate one into the other for an apples-to-apples review.

What is a contractor estimate?

A contractor estimate is a bid to perform the work. Contractors build it from their own costs: crew wages, subcontractor quotes, supplier pricing, equipment, insurance, overhead and the profit they need to stay in business. Many contractors price by the job or by the square rather than by line item.

What contractors account for

  • Visible damage and the work needed to repair it properly
  • Real material quantities, including waste and cut-offs
  • Steep pitches, multiple stories and difficult access
  • Safety requirements and equipment
  • Local code requirements and permits
  • Specialty or discontinued materials
  • Supplier delays and current market prices
  • Project supervision and coordination of trades

A contractor estimate tends to reflect what it really takes to complete the job on your property, but a lump-sum bid can be hard for an adjuster to compare with a line-item estimate.

Xactimate vs contractor estimates: side-by-side comparison

FeatureXactimate estimateContractor estimate
Prepared byAdjuster, appraiser or contractor using softwareThe contractor bidding the job
PurposeValue the covered lossPrice the work to be performed
Pricing basisRegional price list averagesActual costs plus margin
FormatDetailed line items with quantitiesLine items or lump sum
Hidden damageAdded later through supplementsMay include allowances
Overhead and profitApplied separately, sometimes omittedBuilt into the price
Ease of comparisonHigh when both sides use itLower if not itemized

Why do Xactimate and contractor estimates differ?

Different goals

An adjuster's job is to value the covered damage they observed. A contractor's job is to complete the repair correctly and profitably. Neither is necessarily wrong, but they start from different questions. The adjuster asks what the policy owes for the damage documented. The contractor asks what it will cost to deliver a finished, code-compliant repair that carries their warranty.

Scope differences

Scope is usually the biggest source of difference. Contractors often include items that the carrier's estimate leaves out:

  • Drip edge, starter course and ridge cap on roofs
  • Step, counter and apron flashing
  • Ventilation components and pipe jacks
  • Gutters, downspouts and screens
  • Code-required items like underlayment upgrades
  • Detach and reset of satellite dishes, solar panels or fixtures
  • Hidden water damage behind walls or under floors

See common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims for a longer list.

Pricing differences

Even with identical scope, totals can differ. A price list may lag behind post-storm demand, may not reflect specialty materials, or may be dated months before the repair. Contractors price from actual quotes at the time of the job.

Quantity and waste

Roofs with many hips, valleys and dormers waste more material than simple gables. If the carrier applies a lower waste factor than the roof's geometry requires, the material quantity will be short. Measurement differences from aerial reports versus hand measurements also add up.

Overhead and profit

When a job requires a general contractor to coordinate several trades, overhead and profit (often figured as 10 percent each in the industry, though there is no fixed rule) is commonly a legitimate cost. Some carrier estimates omit it, which alone can create a noticeable gap.

Tip: Ask your contractor for an itemized estimate, ideally in Xactimate format. An adjuster can rarely dismiss specific line items with photos and measurements as easily as a single lump-sum number.

Can your insurance company ignore a contractor estimate?

An insurer is not required to pay whatever a contractor bids. It is, however, expected to evaluate the claim reasonably, and a detailed contractor estimate is evidence the adjuster should consider. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 541 prohibits certain unfair settlement practices, such as failing to attempt a fair settlement once liability is reasonably clear.

In practice, carriers respond far better to estimates that match their own format. A contractor estimate that lists line items, quantities and photos of each damaged component is much harder to set aside than a one-page bid. Read more in can your insurance company ignore contractor estimates. This is general information, not legal advice.

How to reconcile Xactimate and contractor estimates

  1. Get both estimates in full, including the carrier's line-item detail and price list date.
  2. Convert to the same format if possible, so line items can be compared directly.
  3. Match items one by one and mark what is missing, what has different quantities and what is priced differently.
  4. Support each difference with photos, measurements, code references or supplier quotes.
  5. Ask for a price list update if the carrier's estimate uses outdated pricing.
  6. Submit a written supplement with the documentation attached.
  7. Escalate to appraisal if the carrier accepts coverage but will not agree on the amount.

What a strong contractor estimate includes

  • Every damaged area listed separately, such as each roof slope, elevation or room
  • Quantities with units: squares, square feet, linear feet or each
  • Unit prices for materials and labor, or a clear breakdown by trade
  • Waste factors explained by the roof's actual geometry
  • Steep-pitch, high-roof and access charges where they apply
  • Code items with the requirement noted
  • Photos referenced to each line item

An estimate built this way gives the adjuster something to verify rather than something to argue with.

Often, the gap between Xactimate vs contractor estimates shrinks dramatically once both are in the same format. What remains is usually a handful of real disagreements that can be negotiated or decided through appraisal. Our article on insurance estimate vs actual repair cost covers related issues like depreciation and hidden damage.

Xactimate and contractor estimates in Texas claims

Texas sees large waves of hail and wind claims each spring across Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio and the Panhandle, plus hurricane claims along the Gulf Coast. After a major storm, demand for roofers and materials surges. That is exactly when gaps between price lists and real contractor pricing tend to widen.

Texas also has specific protections for policyholders. Under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542), insurers generally must accept or reject a claim within 15 business days of receiving requested information and pay within 5 business days after accepting it. Most Texas property policies also contain an appraisal clause, which lets an appraisal panel decide the amount of loss when the two sides cannot agree.

When appraisal resolves estimate disputes

Appraisal is designed for exactly this kind of disagreement: both sides agree the loss is covered but disagree on what it costs. Each party selects an appraiser, the appraisers try to agree on the amount, and an umpire decides any items they cannot settle. Most appraisal panels work in Xactimate or Symbility so every item can be compared directly.

Before invoking appraisal, compare the likely cost with the amount in dispute. Our appraisal cost calculator helps you decide whether the numbers justify it.

Next steps

Do not assume the carrier's Xactimate estimate is final or that your contractor's bid is automatically right. Put both side by side, line by line. Document every missing item, quantity difference and pricing gap, and present the differences in a format the adjuster can verify. That approach resolves many disputes without appraisal, and builds a strong record if you need it.

faqs.a: Xactimate pricing is based on regional market research and is updated regularly, so it is a reasonable baseline for many repairs. It can lag behind real costs after major storms, may not reflect specialty materials and depends on the price list date used. Accuracy also depends on the adjuster capturing the full scope and correct quantities.

It helps. When a contractor's estimate is written in Xactimate or another itemized format, the adjuster can compare it directly with the carrier's estimate. That makes missing items and quantity differences obvious. Lump-sum bids are harder to evaluate and easier for an insurer to discount, even when the price is fair.

faqs.q: What is overhead and profit in an Xactimate estimate?
faqs.a: Overhead and profit covers a general contractor's business costs and margin for coordinating a job. It is applied as a percentage on top of line items, often 10 percent each by industry convention. Carriers commonly include it when a project needs multiple trades, but disputes over whether it applies are frequent.

faqs.q: Why is my contractor's estimate so much higher than the insurance estimate?
faqs.a: The usual causes are scope differences, such as missing flashing, vents or gutters, lower quantities or waste in the carrier estimate, outdated pricing and omitted overhead and profit. Comparing the estimates line by line and documenting each difference is the fastest way to find out how much of the gap is legitimate.

faqs.q: Can appraisal decide between Xactimate and a contractor estimate?
faqs.a: Appraisal decides the amount of loss rather than choosing one estimate over another. The appraisers review the damage and the competing estimates and set values for each item, with an umpire resolving any disagreements. In Texas, appraisers can assess damage but do not decide coverage questions.
